extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and implementation guidance for §§106.44–106.45 of Title IX regulations, covering emergency removals, individualized safety/risk analyses, administrative leave, and the required grievance process protections for complainants and respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized safety or risk analysis for emergency removal (§106.44(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: An individualized, fact-based safety and risk analysis is required before removing a respondent under §106.44(c); removal may occur only where more than a generalized, hypothetical, or speculative belief exists that the respondent poses an immediate threat to someone's physical health or safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis must be individualized with respect to the particular respondent and examine the circumstances "arising from the allegations of sexual harassment." It may include whether violence was involved or other circumstances (e.g., risk of respondent self-harm). The analysis cannot be based on general assumptions about sex, profiling research, or statistical data about allegation frequency. Recipients bear the burden of demonstrating removal met the threshold and may convene trained employees or interdisciplinary threat-assessment teams to conduct the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: High immediate-threat threshold (emergency removals limited to emergencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency removal under §106.44(c) is justified only when there is an immediate threat to physical health or safety; this sets a high threshold intended to permit only emergency removals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department intentionally refrains from further defining what constitutes an emergency so the high threshold remains flexible to various circumstances. The threshold restricts removals to emergency situations and prevents use of §106.44(c) as a pretext for imposing interim suspensions or expulsions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and opportunity to challenge removal (post-removal due process)
rubrics_metrics.description: After an emergency removal, the recipient must provide the respondent notice and an opportunity to challenge the removal; minimal due process requires some kind of notice and an opportunity to be heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations do not require written notice specifically, nor do they add the modifier "meaningful" because an opportunity to be heard appropriate to the circumstances suffices. Recipients have wide latitude to select the procedures for notice and challenge; they may, but need not, use §106.45 procedures. The recipient may place the burden of proof on the respondent in a post-removal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of post-removal procedures and evidence use
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-removal challenge procedures may use some or all procedures in §106.45, but the post-removal process is not strictly required to follow the §106.45 grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts and evidence relied upon in an emergency removal or post-removal challenge may be relevant to a later §106.45 grievance process, but to be relied upon in §106.45 they must meet that provision's requirements (e.g., a witness who provided information in an emergency removal would need to appear and be cross-examined at a §106.45 live hearing for the decision-maker to rely on the statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on basing risk analysis on sex-based generalizations or statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's individualized safety and risk analysis may not be based on general assumptions about sex or research/statistics that profile sex-offense perpetrators or the frequency of false allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis must focus on the particular respondent and circumstances arising from the allegations; reliance on sex-based stereotypes or aggregate data is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR enforcement approach to removals and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR will enforce §106.44(c) fully and will not apply a harmless error standard; violations of §106.44(c) can result in a finding of violation of Title IX/regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will not second-guess recipient decisions that comply with §106.44(c), but may assess whether a recipient's failure to undertake an individualized risk assessment constituted deliberate indifference under §106.44(a). OCR will vigorously enforce Title IX and these regulations regardless of recipient intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion in procedures and burden allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients retain discretion to select the procedures used to provide notice and an opportunity to challenge removals and may place the burden of proof on the respondent in post-removal challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation leaves procedural details to recipients subject to other applicable laws (FERPA, etc.). Use of Title IX personnel trained under §106.45 is permitted for emergency removal decisions or post-removal proceedings, but such involvement could create bias or conflict bars under §106.45(b)(1)(iii) for those individuals in later grievance roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative leave for non-student employees (§106.44(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may place non-student employee respondents on administrative leave during the pendency of a grievance process that complies with §106.45; the provision does not define administrative leave or require it to be paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative leave is generally understood as temporary separation from a job, often with pay and benefits intact, but the regulation does not dictate pay/benefits or require back pay if an employee is later exonerated. State law or contractual obligations may control terms. §106.44(d) permits but does not require administrative leave and does not authorize indefinite leave; administrative leave applies only while a §106.45 grievance process is underway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative leave vs interim suspension and students
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative leave for employees is permitted (and may amount to an interim suspension) whereas interim suspensions of student-respondents are generally prohibited except via emergency removal under §106.44(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations permit — but do not require — administrative leave, including unpaid leave, for employees even though interim suspensions of students are prohibited. Recipients must ensure any such actions do not violate other provisions or laws (e.g., Title VII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-employee considerations for administrative leave
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent is both a student and an employee, placing that person on administrative leave has additional educational-access implications and may be treated differently than for non-student employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing a student-employee on paid administrative leave may be permissible as a supportive measure under §106.30 if it is non-punitive, non-disciplinary, not unreasonably burdensome to the respondent, and otherwise meets the supportive-measures definition. Recipients may choose less burdensome alternatives (e.g., reassignment or supervised contact) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of disability rights in administrative leave
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(d) must not be construed to modify rights under Section 504 or the ADA for employee-respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulations were revised to clarify that administrative leave provisions do not alter disability protections; recipients must comply with disability law obligations in parallel.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.44(a) prohibition on disciplinary sanctions outside §106.45
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may not impose disciplinary sanctions against a respondent without following a grievance process that complies with §106.45; administrative leave without pay is generally considered disciplinary and would likely be prohibited absent §106.44(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must be careful that actions taken while an investigation or grievance is pending do not constitute prohibited disciplinary action under §106.44(a) unless authorized by §106.44(d) or otherwise permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of complainants and respondents may constitute sex discrimination (§106.45(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: How a recipient treats a complainant or a respondent during the grievance process may constitute sex discrimination in violation of Title IX if treatment is based on sex or sex-based stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should avoid sex-based stereotypes, biased training materials, or differential treatment favoring one sex (e.g., crediting only female witnesses or ignoring exonerating evidence for males). The final regulation clarifies that any person, regardless of sex, may be a victim or perpetrator and that unfair procedures may give rise to sex-discrimination claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding institutional bias in grievance processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance processes must be administered without bias favoring complainants or respondents and should be balanced to ensure both sides receive fair procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are advised to have balanced processes, train personnel to avoid bias, and follow §106.45 protections (e.g., trained investigators/decision-makers, conflict-of-interest rules, prompt timelines) to reach accurate outcomes and reduce the risk of sex-discrimination claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required procedural features in §106.45 grievance processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The §106.45 grievance process provides specific procedural protections designed to reach accurate outcomes, including training requirements for investigators/decision-makers, conflict-of-interest prohibitions, and a requirement to conclude the grievance within a designated reasonably prompt time frame (§106.45(b)(1)(v)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While §106.44(c) post-removal procedures need not replicate §106.45, recipients conducting grievance processes under §106.45 must adhere to the enumerated protections (e.g., evidence gathering rules, live hearings with cross-examination where applicable) to ensure fairness and compliance.
